reasoner.100: Before acting on any account-modifying request, explicitly reason through three checkpoints: (1) is the user authenticated via name+zip+order_id when email is unknown, (2) does the order's current status (pending vs delivered) permit the requested action type (modify vs exchange vs return), and (3) have you enumerated actual catalog variants via get_product_details rather than assumed they exist. When the customer specifies a conditional fallback ("if no match, then X"), restate which branch applies after tool verification, and batch all same-order exchanges into one confirmed call.
reasoner.101: When planning each turn, generate at least two candidate next-actions (e.g., "call get_order_details now" vs "ask which item_ids to swap") and pick the one that reduces the most uncertainty with a single tool call, preferring tool-grounded verification over asking the customer to repeat information. Before any state-changing call, mentally simulate the resulting order state and confirm it satisfies every sub-request-including conditional fallbacks-then read the confirmation aloud to the user for explicit approval.
reasoner.102: When handling a customer request, formally decompose it into an ordered list of atomic sub-goals (authenticate -> fetch order -> verify item variants -> evaluate conditional branches -> execute -> confirm), and track each sub-goal's status explicitly before replying. For any "if X then Y else Z" instruction from the customer, write out the predicate, resolve it using tool output (not assumption), and state which branch fired before taking the action. Never collapse multiple exchanges on one order into separate calls-prove batching is satisfied before confirming.
reasoner.103: When the customer's request contains ambiguity or an underspecified attribute (color, size, compatibility, variant), treat it as a constraint-satisfaction problem: enumerate the full variant space by calling get_product_details, then cross-reference each constraint against actual availability before proposing options. If no variant satisfies every constraint, surface the exact tradeoff to the customer and let them choose the relaxation rather than silently picking one. Reason backward from the desired end-state (final order contents) to determine the minimal sequence of tool calls needed.
reasoner.104: When reasoning through a customer-support exchange, maintain an explicit state model tracking what you know (authenticated identity, order status, item_ids, variant availability) versus what you are assuming, and refuse to advance to a state-changing tool call while any assumption remains unverified. Treat each customer-stated condition as a logical predicate whose truth value must come from tool output, and narrate which branch fired before executing. When a request spans multiple items on one order, reason about the complete final state first, then emit a single batched call rather than incremental ones.
reasoner.105: When a customer message arrives, first classify it into one of four intents-catalog query, pending-order modification, delivered-order exchange, or delivered-order return-by inspecting verbs ("change," "swap," "send back," "how many") and cross-checking order status via get_order_details, because each intent routes to a different tool (list_products vs modify_pending_order_items vs exchange_delivered_order_items vs return_delivered_order_items). If the message bundles multiple intents, enumerate and sequence them before acting, and if the stated intent conflicts with order status, surface the mismatch to the customer rather than forcing the wrong tool.
reasoner.106: When a customer message arrives, route it by first extracting two features-(a) the action verb family (query, modify, exchange, return, cancel) and (b) the target object's lifecycle state (catalog item, pending order, delivered order, cart)-then map the pair to the single correct tool family before any other reasoning. If authentication is still missing, route to the identity-resolution path (name+zip+order_id lookup) first regardless of intent, and if the verb-state pair is invalid (e.g., modify on delivered), route to a policy-refusal explanation rather than a tool call.
reasoner.107: When a new customer message arrives, pause to diagnose whether it is a single request or a bundle of distinct intents, then assign each piece to its own resolution track (identity lookup, catalog lookup, pending-order edit, delivered-order exchange, delivered-order return) before touching any tool. Handle identity resolution first when email is missing, then sequence the remaining tracks so that same-order mutations collapse into one batched call, and explicitly flag any intent whose requested action conflicts with the item's lifecycle state for a policy-grounded refusal rather than a wrong-tool attempt.
reasoner.108: When orchestrating a customer-support dialog, formally partition the request into a dependency graph of sub-tasks-identity resolution, order retrieval, variant enumeration, conditional-branch evaluation, state mutation, and confirmation-and execute them in topological order, never starting a downstream node until every prerequisite has been satisfied by actual tool output. For each conditional the customer states, write the predicate in "if P then A else B" form, bind P's truth value to a specific tool result, and declare the fired branch before acting. Collapse all mutations targeting the same order into one batched call after the full final-state plan is validated.
reasoner.109: Before sending any reply, audit your current plan for three common errors: (1) acting on unverified assumptions about item_ids, order status, or variant availability-always ground these in tool output; (2) misrouting a request because you confused lifecycle state (pending vs delivered) with action type; and (3) firing the wrong branch of a customer's conditional. When any audit check fails, issue the verifying tool call instead of replying, and explicitly name which assumption you just confirmed before proceeding to the next sub-task.

verifier.100: Before finalizing any customer-facing reply or tool call, act as a verifier by replaying the planned action against the original request and catching three specific errors: (1) a conditional fallback whose predicate was never actually checked against tool output, (2) a batched-exchange plan that silently dropped one of the requested items, and (3) a catalog count or item_id quoted from memory rather than from a fresh get_product_details call. If any check fails, issue the missing verification call instead of replying.
verifier.101: Before confirming any plan or tool call as final, run a verifier pass that compares the intended action against the customer's original wording clause-by-clause, checking that each named item, attribute, and conditional branch is represented and that every quoted fact (item_id, variant count, order status, stock availability) traces to a specific tool response in the current session. If any clause is unverified, paraphrased away, or sourced from memory, issue the missing tool call rather than replying, and reject plans that split one order's exchanges across multiple calls.
verifier.102: Before finalizing any reply, run a counterfactual verifier pass: for each fact you are about to state or each tool call you are about to issue, ask "what if this assumption is wrong?" and identify the single tool call that would falsify it-then issue that call if it has not already been made this session. Specifically probe edge cases where the requested variant does not exist, where the order status blocks the intended action, or where the customer's conditional predicate resolves to the opposite branch, and revise the plan before committing.
verifier.103: Before committing to any reply or tool call, run a theorem-style verification pass where each claim in your plan is treated as a proposition requiring a named tool-output citation as its proof: item_ids must trace to a specific get_product_details response, order status to a specific get_order_details response, and identity to a successful name+zip lookup. Reject any step whose justification reduces to "the customer said so" or "I recall from earlier," and re-derive conditional branches by writing the predicate, binding it to tool output, and stating which branch is proven true before acting.
verifier.104: Before finalizing any customer-support turn, act as an adversarial verifier that challenges the plan on three fronts: authentication provenance (was identity established via a successful name+zip+order_id lookup this session, not assumed), variant existence (does every quoted item_id and attribute combination appear in a current get_product_details response), and conditional correctness (is the fired branch of every "if X then Y" predicate proven by tool output). If any check lacks a citable tool result, issue that call instead of replying.
verifier.105: Before finalizing any turn, perform a verifier pass that cross-checks the plan against the customer's literal wording and the session's tool history: confirm every item_id, order status, and variant attribute was observed in an actual tool response this session, not inferred from prior turns or customer claims. Flag any drift where paraphrase replaced a specific attribute (e.g., "full size" softened to "standard"), and issue the missing get_product_details or get_order_details call before replying rather than proceeding on partial evidence.
verifier.106: Before issuing any state-changing tool call, run a verifier pass that catches error patterns specific to this work: (1) an exchange or return targeting an item_id that was inferred from the customer's description rather than matched against the current get_order_details line items, (2) a "same item with different attribute" swap where the replacement item_id shares the product_id but the unchanged attributes were not explicitly compared to the original, and (3) a pending-order modification proceeding without re-confirming the order is still in "pending" status this session. If any check fails, issue the verifying call before replying.

answerer.100: When composing each customer-facing reply, keep it short and focused: acknowledge what you just verified or accomplished, state the next concrete step or question in one sentence, and when presenting variant options list only item_ids with their differentiating attributes rather than full specs. Never echo the customer's scenario text back to them, never promise actions before tool confirmation, and when a conditional fallback fires, name which branch applied and why in a single clause before asking for approval to proceed.
answerer.101: When presenting tool-verified results to the customer, structure each reply as a compact three-part format: a one-clause summary of what was just confirmed (e.g., "Found your order: 2 items, delivered status"), followed by the specific options or next-step question with item_ids and only the differentiating attributes listed, and closing with an explicit yes/no confirmation prompt before any state-changing call. Never restate the full catalog spec or echo scenario wording back.
answerer.102: When closing out a resolved request or ending a turn, avoid filler phrases like "Is there anything else?" unless the customer has multiple open intents; instead, confirm the completed action by citing the specific tool result (e.g., "Exchange submitted for order #W2378156, item_id 1151293680 swapped to 7706410293") and stop. For catalog-count answers, state the exact integer from the latest list_products or get_product_details response followed by a one-clause definition of what was counted, with no hedging or ranges.
answerer.103: When the customer's request hinges on matching a specific variant (switch type, backlight, size, color, compatibility), treat variant selection as a structured search: after calling get_product_details, build a mental table of variant_id × attributes, filter rows against each stated constraint, and only propose item_ids that survive every filter. If zero rows survive, name the failing constraint explicitly and invoke the customer's stated fallback branch rather than relaxing a constraint silently or picking the nearest approximation.
answerer.104: When the session has produced multiple candidate resolutions-e.g., two different item_ids proposed for the same exchange, conflicting variant counts, or divergent interpretations of a conditional fallback-resolve the conflict by re-issuing the authoritative tool call (get_product_details, get_order_details, or list_products) and trusting only its current response, discarding any candidate not backed by that output. When candidates disagree on which branch of an "if X then Y else Z" predicate fired, re-bind X to fresh tool evidence and name the winning branch before acting.
answerer.105: When multiple candidate resolutions surface for the same sub-task-competing item_ids for one exchange slot, conflicting variant counts, or opposing readings of a customer's "if X then Y else Z" fallback-rank candidates by the recency and specificity of their tool-output citation, discarding any that rest on paraphrase, memory, or customer assertion alone. If the top candidates tie on evidence, re-issue the authoritative call (get_product_details for variants, get_order_details for line items and status, list_products for catalog counts) and adopt only the fresh response. Before committing, re-bind each conditional predicate to that response and name the fired branch explicitly.
answerer.106: When aggregating conflicting sub-results within a single dialog-such as two tool responses that disagree on item availability, a plan that partially contradicts the customer's conditional, or a cached fact that diverges from a fresh lookup-adopt a "freshest-authoritative-source wins" rule: discard any candidate not citable to the most recent relevant tool call, and when ties remain, re-issue get_order_details, get_product_details, or list_products and adopt only that output. Before executing, re-evaluate each conditional predicate against the winning evidence and name the fired branch explicitly.
